1 --- 2 title: Designing view transitions 3 description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app. 4 nav_title: View transitions 5 --- 6 7 In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that. 8 9 Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states. 10 11 React's `` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions. 12 13 This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route. 14 15 ## Example 16 17 As an example, we'll build a photography gallery called _Frames_. 18 19 We'll start by morphing a thumbnail into a hero image (shared elements), then animate the loading skeleton into real content (Suspense reveals), add directional slides for forward and back navigation (route transitions), and finish with crossfades for switching between photographer tabs (same-route transitions). 20 21 You can find the resources used in this example here: 22 23 - [Demo](https://react-view-transitions-demo.labs.vercel.dev) 24 - [Code](https://github.com/vercel-labs/react-view-transitions-demo) 25 26 Before starting, enable view transitions in your Next.js config: 27 28 ```ts filename="next.config.ts" 29 import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 30 31 const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 32 experimental: { 33 viewTransition: true, 34 }, 35 } 36 37 export default nextConfig 38 ``` 39 40 App Router uses [React canary releases](https://react.dev/blog/2023/05/03/react-canaries), which contain all stable React 19 changes as well as newer features like `ViewTransition`. You do not need to install `react@canary` yourself. 41 42 > [!NOTE] 43 > The View Transitions API is supported in all major browsers, though some animations may behave differently in Safari. Without browser support, your application works normally, the transitions simply do not animate. 44 45 Then import the `ViewTransition` component from React: 46 47 ```tsx 48 import { ViewTransition } from 'react' 49 ``` 50 51 `` animations are activated by [Transitions](https://react.dev/reference/react/useTransition), [``](https://react.dev/reference/react/Suspense), and [`useDeferredValue`](https://react.dev/reference/react/useDeferredValue). Regular `setState` calls do not trigger them. In Next.js, route navigations are transitions, so `` animations activate automatically during navigation. 52 53 ### Step 1: Morph a thumbnail into a hero image 54 55 The gallery displays photos in a grid. Clicking a photo opens a detail page with a larger version of the same image. Without transitions, the thumbnail disappears and the hero appears. Nothing connects them visually. The user has to scan the detail page to confirm they clicked the right photo. 56 57 In motion design, when an object persists across a cut, it communicates continuity. The viewer understands they are looking at the same thing, not a replacement. This is the most important transition pattern: **shared element morphing**. 58 59 Wrap both the grid thumbnail and the detail hero in `` with the same `name`: 60 61 ```tsx filename="components/photo-grid.tsx" 62 import { ViewTransition } from 'react' 63 import Image from 'next/image' 64 import Link from 'next/link' 65 66 function PhotoGrid({ photos }) { 67 return ( 68
69 {photos.map((photo) => ( 70 71 72 73 74 75 ))} 76
77 ) 78 } 79 ``` 80 81 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/photo-content.tsx" 82 import { ViewTransition } from 'react' 83 import Image from 'next/image' 84 85 async function PhotoContent({ id }) { 86 const photo = await getPhoto(id) 87 88 return ( 89 90 91 92 ) 93 } 94 ``` 95 96 The `name` prop creates identity. React finds elements with the same name on the old and new pages, then animates between their size and position automatically. No additional props are needed for the morph to work. 97 98 If we click a thumbnail now, the image scales and repositions from its grid cell to the hero slot. Navigating back reverses the morph. The user sees one object moving, not two objects swapping. 99 100 #### Customizing the morph animation 101 102 The morph works without any CSS. To customize it, add `share="morph"`. This assigns the `morph` class to the view transition, which you can target with CSS pseudo-elements. For example, to soften the morph mid-flight with a [`blur`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/filter-function/blur) keyframe: 103 104 ```tsx 105 106 107 108 ``` 109 110 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 111 ::view-transition-group(.morph) { 112 animation-duration: 400ms; 113 } 114 ::view-transition-image-pair(.morph) { 115 animation-name: via-blur; 116 } 117 @keyframes via-blur { 118 30% { 119 filter: blur(3px); 120 } 121 } 122 ``` 123 124 The blur hides pixel-level interpolation artifacts during the transition. At 400ms, the morph is slow enough to register but fast enough to feel direct. 125 126 ### Step 2: Animate loading states with Suspense reveals 127 128 The photo detail page loads its content asynchronously. While data is in flight, a Suspense boundary shows a skeleton. When the data resolves, the skeleton is replaced by the real content. 129 130 Without a transition, the swap is instant. The skeleton vanishes and the content pops in. 131 132 In motion design, vertical direction encodes hierarchy. Content sliding up communicates arrival. Content sliding down communicates departure. The pair together creates a handoff: the placeholder yields to the real thing. 133 134 Wrap the Suspense fallback in a `ViewTransition` with an exit animation, and the content in a `ViewTransition` with an enter animation: 135 136 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/page.tsx" 137 import { Suspense, ViewTransition } from 'react' 138 139 export default async function PhotoPage({ params }) { 140 const { id } = await params 141 142 return ( 143 146 147 148 } 149 > 150 151 152 153 154 ) 155 } 156 ``` 157 158 The `default="none"` prop prevents this `ViewTransition` from animating during unrelated transitions, like the shared element morph from Step 1. Without it, every transition on the page would trigger every `ViewTransition`'s animation. 159 160 The CSS animations use asymmetric timing. The exit is fast (150ms). The enter is slower (210ms) and delayed until the exit completes: 161 162 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 163 :root { 164 --duration-exit: 150ms; 165 --duration-enter: 210ms; 166 } 167 168 ::view-transition-old(.slide-down) { 169 animation: 170 var(--duration-exit) ease-out both fade reverse, 171 var(--duration-exit) ease-out both slide-y reverse; 172 } 173 ::view-transition-new(.slide-up) { 174 animation: 175 var(--duration-enter) ease-in var(--duration-exit) both fade, 176 400ms ease-in both slide-y; 177 } 178 179 @keyframes fade { 180 from { 181 filter: blur(3px); 182 opacity: 0; 183 } 184 to { 185 filter: blur(0); 186 opacity: 1; 187 } 188 } 189 @keyframes slide-y { 190 from { 191 transform: translateY(10px); 192 } 193 to { 194 transform: translateY(0); 195 } 196 } 197 ``` 198 199 The asymmetry is deliberate. Old content should leave quickly so it does not compete for attention. New content should arrive more gently so the user has time to register it. The `var(--duration-exit)` delay on the enter animation means the new content waits for the old content to finish leaving before it appears. 200 201 If we refresh the page, the skeleton slides down and fades out, and a moment later the real content slides up and fades in. 202 203 ### Step 3: Add directional motion for navigation 204 205 The gallery now has morphing images and animated loading states. But navigating between pages still has no directional signal. Forward and back navigations look identical. The user cannot tell from the animation whether they moved deeper into the app or returned to a previous page. 206 207 In film and animation, horizontal direction encodes spatial position. Moving left means progressing forward (like turning a page in a left-to-right language). Moving right means going back. This convention is so ingrained that violating it feels disorienting. 208 209 Use the `transitionTypes` prop on `` to tag forward navigations: 210 211 ```tsx filename="components/photo-grid.tsx" 212 213 {/* photo thumbnail */} 214 215 ``` 216 217 The same pattern works for any navigation within the app. For example, previous/next arrows on a photo detail page can use `nav-back` and `nav-forward` to animate in the corresponding direction. 218 219 For links that return the user to a previous page, use `nav-back`: 220 221 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/page.tsx" 222 223 ← Gallery 224 225 ``` 226 227 The transition type is not automatic. You decide which links are "forward" and which are "back" based on your app's navigation hierarchy. 228 229 Then wrap page content in a `ViewTransition` that maps transition types to directional animations: 230 231 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/page.tsx" 232 245 {/* page content */} 246 247 ``` 248 249 The `enter` and `exit` props accept an object keyed by transition type. When a navigation carries the `nav-forward` type, the exit animation slides old content left and the enter animation slides new content in from the right. The `default: "none"` ensures that transitions without a type (like initial page loads) produce no animation. 250 251 The CSS for directional slides: 252 253 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 254 ::view-transition-old(.nav-forward) { 255 --slide-offset: -60px; 256 animation: 257 150ms ease-in both fade reverse, 258 400ms ease-in-out both slide reverse; 259 } 260 ::view-transition-new(.nav-forward) { 261 --slide-offset: 60px; 262 animation: 263 210ms ease-out 150ms both fade, 264 400ms ease-in-out both slide; 265 } 266 267 ::view-transition-old(.nav-back) { 268 --slide-offset: 60px; 269 animation: 270 150ms ease-in both fade reverse, 271 400ms ease-in-out both slide reverse; 272 } 273 ::view-transition-new(.nav-back) { 274 --slide-offset: -60px; 275 animation: 276 210ms ease-out 150ms both fade, 277 400ms ease-in-out both slide; 278 } 279 280 @keyframes slide { 281 from { 282 translate: var(--slide-offset); 283 } 284 to { 285 translate: 0; 286 } 287 } 288 ``` 289 290 The 60px offset is enough to communicate direction without making the user track a fast-moving element across the screen. 291 292 #### Anchoring the header 293 294 During directional slides, the header should not move. A sliding header breaks the user's spatial anchor. They need one fixed reference point to understand that the _content_ moved, not the entire viewport. 295 296 Assign the header a `viewTransitionName` and suppress its animation in CSS: 297 298 ```tsx filename="components/header.tsx" 299
300 {/* navigation links */} 301
302 ``` 303 304 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 305 ::view-transition-group(site-header) { 306 animation: none; 307 z-index: 100; 308 } 309 ::view-transition-old(site-header) { 310 display: none; 311 } 312 ::view-transition-new(site-header) { 313 animation: none; 314 } 315 ``` 316 317 The `display: none` on the old snapshot prevents a flash where both old and new headers are briefly visible. The `z-index: 100` ensures the header renders above the sliding content. 318 319 If we navigate forward to a photo, content slides left. If we click the "← Gallery" link (tagged with `nav-back`), content slides right. The header stays fixed throughout both transitions. 320 321 Browser-initiated back navigations (the back button or swipe gestures) do not carry a transition type, so the directional slide does not play. The shared element morph from Step 1 still applies if both pages have matching `name` props. 322 323 #### Respecting reduced motion 324 325 Directional slides simulate physical movement across the viewport. This is the most common trigger for motion sensitivity. Morphs, reveals, and crossfades carry less risk since they affect smaller areas or rely on opacity rather than position. 326 327 The simplest approach is to disable all animation durations: 328 329 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 330 @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { 331 ::view-transition-old(*), 332 ::view-transition-new(*), 333 ::view-transition-group(*) { 334 animation-duration: 0s !important; 335 animation-delay: 0s !important; 336 } 337 } 338 ``` 339 340 Without animation, content swaps instantly, which is the browser's default behavior. A more refined approach would preserve crossfades and opacity transitions while removing positional movement. See ["No Motion Isn't Always prefers-reduced-motion"](https://css-tricks.com/nuking-motion-with-prefers-reduced-motion/) for more on this. 341 342 ### Step 4: Crossfade content within the same route 343 344 The gallery has a photographer section with tabs. Each tab shows a different photographer's photos, but the route structure is the same: `/collection/[slug]`. Clicking between tabs does not feel like navigating to a new page. It feels like switching content within the same container. 345 346 A directional slide would be wrong here. Slides communicate "going to a new place." A crossfade communicates "same place, different content." The container persists (continuity), only the grid inside changes (swap). 347 348 Use a `ViewTransition` with `key` set to the current slug. When the key changes, React triggers a transition between the old and new content: 349 350 ```tsx filename="app/collection/[slug]/page.tsx" 351 import { Suspense, ViewTransition } from 'react' 352 353 export default async function CollectionPage({ params }) { 354 const { slug } = await params 355 356 return ( 357 }> 358 365 366 367 368 ) 369 } 370 ``` 371 372 The `share="auto"` and `enter="auto"` props tell React to use its default crossfade animation. The `name` prop gives the container an identity so React knows what to animate. The `key={slug}` change is what triggers the transition. 373 374 If we click between photographer tabs, the grid crossfades. The tab bar and surrounding layout do not move. Only the photo grid transitions between states. 375 376 ## Next steps 377 378 You now know how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation. Shared elements communicate continuity across routes. Suspense reveals animate loading handoffs. Directional slides encode navigation history. Crossfades signal content changes within the same location. 379 380 Each pattern answers a different question for the user: 381 382 | Pattern | What it communicates | 383 | ---------------------- | ------------------------------- | 384 | Shared element (morph) | "Same thing, going deeper" | 385 | Suspense reveal | "Data loaded" | 386 | Directional slide | "Going forward / coming back" | 387 | Same-route crossfade | "Same place, different content" | 388 389 For API details and more patterns: 390 391 - [View transition configuration](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/viewTransition) 392 - [Link `transitionTypes` prop](/docs/app/api-reference/components/link#transitiontypes) 393 - [`useRouter`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/use-router), which also supports `transitionTypes` in `push()` and `replace()` 394 - [React `ViewTransition` component](https://react.dev/reference/react/ViewTransition) 395 - [Complete CSS from this guide](https://github.com/vercel-labs/react-view-transitions-demo/blob/main/src/app/globals.css) — all keyframes and view transition rules in one file 396

1	---
2	title: viewTransition
3	description: Enable ViewTransition API from React in App Router
4	version: experimental
5	---
6	
7	`viewTransition` enables React's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) integration in Next.js. This lets you animate navigations, loading states, and content changes using the native browser View Transitions API.
8	
9	To enable this feature, you need to set the `viewTransition` property to `true` in your `next.config.js` file.
10	
11	```js filename="next.config.js"
12	/** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */
13	const nextConfig = {
14	  experimental: {
15	    viewTransition: true,
16	  },
17	}
18	
19	module.exports = nextConfig
20	```
21	
22	> [!NOTE]
23	> The [`<ViewTransition>`](https://react.dev/reference/react/ViewTransition) component is provided by React.
24	> The `experimental.viewTransition` flag enables Next.js integration, such as triggering
25	> transitions during route navigations.
26	
27	## Usage
28	
29	You can import the [`<ViewTransition>` Component](https://react.dev/reference/react/ViewTransition) from React in your application:
30	
31	```jsx
32	import { ViewTransition } from 'react'
33	```
34	
35	### Live Demo
36

file.content:
---
title: viewTransition
description: Enable ViewTransition API from React in App Router
version: experimental
---

`viewTransition` enables React's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) integration in Next.js. This lets you animate navigations, loading states, and content changes using the native browser View Transitions API.

To enable this feature, you need to set the `viewTransition` property to `true` in your `next.config.js` file.

```js filename="next.config.js"
/** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */
const nextConfig = {
  experimental: {
    viewTransition: true,
  },
}

module.exports = nextConfig
```

> [!NOTE]
> The [`<ViewTransition>`](https://react.dev/reference/react/ViewTransition) component is provided by React.
> The `experimental.viewTransition` flag enables Next.js integration, such as triggering
> transitions during route navigations.

## Usage

You can import the [`<ViewTransition>` Component](https://react.dev/reference/react/ViewTransition) from React in your application:

```jsx
import { ViewTransition } from 'react'
```

### Live Demo

Check out the [View Transitions Demo](https://react-view-transitions-demo.labs.vercel.dev) to see this feature in action, or read the [designing view transitions guide](/docs/app/guides/view-transitions) for a step-by-step walkthrough.

The View Transitions API is a baseline web standard, and browser support continues to expand. As React's [`<ViewTransition>`](https://react.dev/reference/react/ViewTransition) component evolves, more transition patterns and use cases will become available.

content.text:
All changes are in place. Here's what was added:

**`next.config.ts`** — enabled `experimental.viewTransition`.

**Shared element morph** (`ProductGrid.tsx`, `product/[slug]/page.tsx`) — both the thumbnail and hero wrap the colored box in `<ViewTransition name={`product-image-${slug}`} share="morph">`. The browser animates size/position between the two.

**Directional slides** — grid `Link`s carry `transitionTypes={['nav-forward']}`; the back link carries `['nav-back']`. Each page's root `<ViewTransition>` maps those types to `nav-forward`/`nav-back` classes targeted by CSS (`slide` + `fade` keyframes, ±60px offset).

**Suspense reveal** — the fallback is wrapped in `<ViewTransition exit="slide-down">` and the content in `<ViewTransition enter="slide-up" default="none">`, with 150ms exit / 210ms delayed enter for a clean handoff.

**Reduced motion** — a `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` block zeroes out animation duration/delay on all view-transition pseudo-elements, letting content swap instantly.
